newsitem.title: UK: BBC gives qualified welcome to digital TV rules.
newsitem.headline: BBC gives qualified welcome to digital TV rules.

text.p: The BBC said on Tuesday that digital television rules put before the British parliament were a "step in the right direction" but warned that they relied heavily on watchdog OFTEL's ability to enforce an open market.

The BBC was responding after the government's Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) set out final regulations for a regime to license digital receiver set-top boxes. These rules are set to come into force on January 7.
"These proposals are a welcome step in the right direction. But consumers and broadcasters still face uncertainty if OFTEL is not able to enforce an open market," said BBC Director-General John Birt.
The BBC welcomed the government's decision to require information about the specifications of the set-top boxes to be released to broadcasters as soon as it is available.
It said that broadcasters planning to compete with programme services provided by the set-top box operator would be able to deliver those services from the start of digital broadcasting.
BSkyB, the dominant force in British pay television, is planning to launch a digital satellite service with up to 200 channels in late 1997.
Digital terrestrial television -- broadcast from land-based transmitters -- is set to begin in mid-1998, offering a further 35 or so channels.
Some broadcasters had expressed fears that BSkyB would be able to exploit its "first-mover" status to gain a stranglehold on the digital environment.

Digital television will transform British broadcasting and communications by creating the hundreds of new channels and allowing for the creation of interactive services such as home banking and shopping.
To receive any of the new services, audiences will need a digital receiver -- available first as a "set-top" box and later inside digital televisions.
The BBC, which is planning a series of digital subscription channels, has said it will seek to make them available by all delivery means -- cable, satellite and terrestrial.
"In particular, much remains to be done to ensure that all digital receiving equipment - cable, satellite and terrestrial - will be compatible," Birt said.
